text.en: The Mashgiach reads 'Bereishis is also a maamar' as showing that the first maamar is so lofty it never descended into the words 'vayomer', and he parallels the hidden first three maamaros with the three hidden nations promised to Avraham.

He makes the ten weeks from Shiva Asar B'Tammuz to Rosh Hashanah parallel the ten nations, so that the Three Weeks are the 'Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni' of the year, destined to become its most joyful days.

The Mashgiach proposes that Rashi's 'koach maasav higid l'amo' answers the nations by revealing that Klal Yisrael is destined for the Kadmoni, Esav's realm and the whole world, so complaining over the seven nations is beside the point.
Gimmel-Reish, used in the sefarim for the first three, is read by the Mashgiach as Gad and Reuven, the two tribes bound to 'reishis' and to the geulah.

Following Rav Shimshon of Ostropoli, the forty days of the spies, which are Tammuz and the nine days, are the domain of the Samech Mem, hinted in the letters preceding 'anavim'; when Har Esav is judged, 'anavim' will be complete with its yud.
Like belief in techiyas hameisim, which the Mashgiach calls a sign rather than a punishment, the tribes' instinctive desire for this land was a sign that their souls belonged to the days of Moshiach.
The washing out of every blemish in the time of tikun may be why one does not wash during the nine days, since they are not yet that time.
Aharon's kehunah was a gift, while Pinchas's was earned, because he atoned for Klal Yisrael, which exists for all generations; therefore his kehunah too is for all generations.

Moshe Rabbeinu could not avenge Zimri's act, because as the leader standing above the people his act would not have meant that the people itself took revenge; it needed a simple man from within the people.

Following Chassidic seforim, the Mashgiach says Zimri largely meant it for the sake of Heaven, but one small crumb of personal reckoning spoiled him, and that sinning part of the soul is what was called Zimri.
The masses of plain Jews who searched for the lost child did what Pinchas did: they showed the holiness of Klal Yisrael and its separation from whoever has a foreign growth attached to him.
Eliyahu equals 'ben' (son) in gematria, and through him it will become clear that Jews are children of Hashem.
Each of the moadim represents one of the midos of the Avos, and these are the traits Jews showed this week: merciful, modest and doing kindness.

The drash is the depth of the pshat: the Torah tells of Bilam foolishly cursing Moav for money, which only cleared the way for Israel, to show the lowliness of one ruled by desire; the drash draws the opposite, that those who rule their yetzer make a cheshbon of what will come later.

Since Bilam was Lavan, he knew that Lavan's blessing to Rivka had caused Hashem to delay her children so that Israel's blessing would not be credited to him; Bilam wished to bless Israel so that their blessing would likewise be held back.

The land Sichon took from Moav belongs to Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni, corresponding to Binah, the place where judgments are sweetened, which is why Bilam's curse of Moav turned into a blessing for Israel.

Og, descended from the Nefilim, survived the Flood by clinging to the outside of the teiva, while Noach was inside it; seeing the Anakim in Chevron taught Kalev that in a generation of Nefilim one survives only by grasping the inner teiva, the words of tefillah.
The Mashgiach reads the command to make a light for the teiva in two ways: to make the word shine and to set a gem in it, since every word of tefillah both gives light and is a diamond.
One cries out in tefillah not so that Hashem will hear but so that we will hear; in a time when everyone is spiritually asleep, the shouting is what wakes a person.

The two hundred heads of Sanhedrin from Yissachar date from the time of the second Beis Hamikdash, after Torah had been forgotten in Bavel, so they show the effect of having camped next to Moshe a thousand years earlier.

The Mashgiach reads Zimri's act through the Arizal on Shlomo HaMelech: taking a king's daughter was an attempt to draw her whole nation under the Shechinah, which is why the angels, awaiting the end of days, sided with Zimri.

Zimri's error is repaired in reverse in Rabbi Akiva: Zimri risked turning Jewish seed into gentile seed, and Rabbi Akiva came into the world from converts, gentile seed that became Jewish, and married the wife of Turnus Rufus after a proper conversion.

Pinchas's reward fits his act exactly: because he guarded the Jewish body from mixing with the seed of the serpent, his own body was purified as at Sinai, so he lives on in the body and may enter the Holy of Holies.
The small yud in Pinchas's name stands for the smallest point of Jewishness, which even the lowest Jew carries and which will one day flare into a great flame.

The Kosel Maaravi corresponds to the point of Avraham Avinu in every Jew: the Even Shesiyah extends to it, so in a time of destruction it is the place one can still reach, as the point in the heart is.

Nadav and Avihu's strange fire was an attempt to hasten what must come as fire from heaven; their souls entered Pinchas so that he would repair it, and like Eliyahu he must wait for the Beis HaMikdash to descend in fire.
Pinchas merited precisely because he was small: Hashem chose a moment when even the Sanhedrin, the nesi'im and Moshe Rabbeinu stood by, to show that greatness is not the monopoly of the great.

Klal Yisrael is like a rope: the higher the elevated Jew climbs, the more he pulls the simple Jew up, and when he lowers himself, the end of the rope falls even lower; so 'Yisrael', the elevated, sitting in idleness led 'ha'am' to the worst sins.

On 'ki gamar chasid, ki pasu emunim' the Mashgiach brings both readings, that the chassid's fall caused the people's emunah to fail and that the people's fall dragged down the chassid, and says both are true.
A mashpia comes from 'shipua', a slope: influence flows downward from the higher one, but one must be careful not to slide down oneself.
One who does not hear the song of creation is like a deaf man at a wedding who thinks the dancers mad; to him those who sway in davening look crazy.
Melamdim are compared to stars because a star looks like a tiny dot yet is far larger than the earth; so a melamed seems small in people's eyes but is truly great.

The contradiction between Devarim and Shelach is resolved by both being true: Hashem commanded Moshe to send the meraglim precisely so that they could go as His shluchim rather than as shluchim of a people with impure intentions, and their failure lay in not staying bound to that sending.

Yosef's brothers were the first meraglim: by going down to Mitzrayim unknowingly and withstanding its tests, they, like Yosef and Sarah before them, left an imprint of kedushah that later let all of Israel keep their purity there.

The 'treasures hidden by the Canaanim' are the kedushah of Eretz Yisrael covered over by kelipah; the command 'dig out the land' meant uncovering it through Torah, avodah and mesiras nefesh, which the Mashgiach likens to a bris milah of the land.

The permutation of Hashem's Name for Tammuz is the only one drawn from Megillas Esther, from Haman's words, and since the whole theme of the Megillah is 'venahafoch hu', the reversed permutation itself hints that it can be turned around to good.

Kalev of Yehudah and Yehoshua of Yosef, the two who did not fail among the meraglim, are the tribes of Moshiach ben Dovid and Moshiach ben Yosef; whoever does not fail in the 'territory' of Tammuz and Av likewise brings Moshiach.
Tzitzis equals all the mitzvos because each mitzvah forms only a piece of the soul's future garment, while tzitzis is itself a complete garment and so includes the whole.
Pinchas knew his act might cost him the kehunah, yet he went ahead only to make a kiddush Hashem; his reward of kehunah came from the act itself, not from being Aharon's grandson.
The point of 'in their midst' is that the zealotry belonged to Klal Yisrael as a whole: Pinchas acted as a simple Jew among them, so that through him the people itself was zealous.
The Mashgiach reads Zimri's name as the one small part of the soul that sinned out of a personal calculation, a foreign growth on a Jew, while the people as a whole stay separate from it.
Eliyahu is gematria 'ben' (son), and the word Eliyahu appears nine times in the haftarah; through Eliyahu it will be clarified that Jews are Hashem's children.
The child did not suffer on account of others, nor did the family suffer on his account: he came into the world for this, as part of his own tikkun.
Aharon's praise of 'not changing' is read as a choice: every day he picked the avodah of the lamps, tied to Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim, over the ketores, tied to wealth.
The Mashgiach sharpens the praise: in forty years Aharon did not give up the lamps even one day to gain some wealth, though a father needs money to marry off his children.
At the bris the Mashgiach sees ketores and lamps together: a home bringing a child into the covenant of Avraham Avinu is wished both Torah and greatness at once.
The holy words Bilaam spoke did not truly come out of his own mouth: Hashem set a foreign thing in it as a barrier, and the words came out from that.
Rashi and the Targum read 'shesum ha'ayin' at opposite extremes, one as a blinded eye and one as sharp sight, and the Ba'al Shem Tov shows how both are true of Bilaam.
According to the Ba'al Shem Tov, Bilaam's blind eye was Hashem's doing, so that he could not cause harm with it.

Ur Kasdim was self-sacrifice for a G-d Avraham had never seen; the Akeidah was harder because he had come to know Hashem as Emes over many years, and now saw Him only 'from a distance', as if the One he knew was not keeping His word.

Avraham could not see the simple answer a child learning Rashi sees, not for lack of wisdom, but because the test required that he not know: when Hashem does not want a person to know, he does not know.
The same answer resolves how Haman, brilliant enough to calculate that Moshe died on the seventh of Adar, missed that Moshe was also born then: Hashem wanted there to be Purim.

Applying the Ramban's principle to the ten tests, the Mashgiach says each era of Jewish history could be matched to one of Avraham's tests, and the last stretch of the golus corresponds to the Akeidah, a test of hester panim and kashyos.

The word Emes, which the Torah does not write after the parshiyos of Shema but which we add ourselves, corresponds to the 'eikev', the heels of Moshiach, when the truth cannot be seen; hence Avraham was told 'eikev asher shamata bekoli'.

The Mashgiach compares the Jew's belief in Hashem to the inherited knowledge of the beaver and the spider: it is not learned but part of his organism, and with Avraham a species carrying this trait began.

Since Avraham was not a continuation of mankind from Adam and Noach, he and Sarah needed a newly created power to have children, and he was told he need not honor his father, as he was not truly his father.
The man of Bereishis belongs in the land of Bereishis: Eretz Yisrael, the place from which the globe developed, is the natural home of the first Jew.
Hashem's first words to Avraham, the attribute of chesed, were a positive command to go to the land, while His first words to Yitzchak, the attribute of din, were a prohibition against leaving it.
Applying the Maharal on Moshe's parents, the Mashgiach explains that the Torah omits Avraham's merits because the Jewish nation's existence is a necessity, not a reward.

The Mashgiach reads the Ramban's harsh judgment of Avraham as deliberate: by showing at the outset that Avraham could sin and still be chosen, it teaches that the Jewish nation does not rest on anyone's righteousness.
Avraham's descent to Mitzrayim and Sarah's steadfastness in Pharaoh's house prepared the purity that kept the Jewish women holy in Mitzrayim.

Cheshvan's combination of Hashem's Name is the only one drawn across two pesukim, from 'u'dvash' that ends a passage into 'hayom hazeh' that opens a new one, teaching that the honey of Tishrei must be carried over into the month of decay.
'Av HaRachaman', the merciful Father, has the gematria of 'dvash', honey, 306: in Tishrei Hashem appears to us as sweetness.

Every person governs his own portion of creation; Noach's portion was the animals that came into the Teivah, which stayed pure amid a corrupt world, and geographically Eretz Yisrael, where no Mabul fell.
The Teivah, built with halachos to exact dimensions like the Mishkan, was not a ship but a place of kedushah, an embassy of heaven on earth, and so the Mabul's law of destruction did not apply to it.

Life in food is the word of Hashem; the purer a creature, the more it extracts from less, so the tzaddik eats little and the sheep lives on grass, while the cruel lion must eat concentrated food, meat.
The lion's attack on Noach was a result of Cham's sin, which repeated Adam's sin inside the Teivah, brought back the curse and made the lion need meat again.
Hashem makes three tries: the worlds of Adam and of Noach were spoiled, and the third world, like the third Beis HaMikdash, will be perfect.

The 'ach' of 'only Noach remained' carries a double message: Rashi reads it as Noach's injury from the lion, and the Mashgiach adds that the verse no longer calls him tzaddik, because Cham's sin had affected him.
The animals that came to the Teva were the 'tzaddikim' of the animal world: they belonged to Noach's portion of creation, which his righteousness kept from corruption.

The Mashgiach reconciles the Ibn Ezra and Chazal on the lion's food: in the Teva's pure society the lion could live on straw, as before Adam's sin and in the days of Moshiach, and only after Cham's sin did it need meat.
The more physical a being is, the more concentrated food it needs; a lion's one meal of meat equals a week of a cow's grazing, so a world fallen from its purity needs meat.
Noach's drinking is read as a mistake about the times: he thought the era of Moshiach had come, when one can drink a great cup of wine without becoming drunk, like the cup of Eliyahu at the Seder.
The parsha is built like a headline: its opening verses already say that Noach was saved only by grace, and it moves from Noach to Avraham Avinu, in whose merit the world survived.

The root of bracha spells doubling in three orders of magnitude: beis is two, chaf twenty, reish two hundred, as alef is one; this is why Yosef, the sixth of the ushpizin, had his blessing doubled into two shevatim.

Time is a creation: each day comes down, is inscribed with what a person does, and ascends; therefore teshuvah is easier before the day goes up, at night before sleep, on Erev Shabbos and on Erev Rosh Hashanah.
Rashi's 'thirteen' is not a misprint: the boys became bar mitzvah-grown not by age but by what they absorbed on the day of Avraham's passing, Yaakov from Avraham's days and Esav from Nimrod's tumah.
Yaakov's words 'sell me as this day' mean that the very nature of that day, which made Esav a denier of the World to Come, showed that he had no use for the bechorah.
Onkelos and Rashi do not disagree: Yitzchak loved Esav for the food he ate from his hunting, and that was Esav's deception, since the food with its kedushah was really Yaakov's.
Yitzchak concluded from the kedushah in the food that Esav was a concealed tzaddik, one of the thirty-six, who is greater than a revealed one; this is why he favored him.
The three letters of bracha each mean addition at a different level: beis is one becoming two, chaf is ten becoming twenty, reish is a hundred becoming two hundred.
Six is bracha: Yosef, whose name means adding, is the sixth of the Ushpizin, and Toldos, the sixth sedra, is the sedra filled with bracha.
'Michra kayom' means 'sell according to today': by Esav's philosophy of today the bechorah is worthless, by Yaakov's it is worth everything, so the sale fits both views.
Eliyahu could give Elisha double what he had because on his last day all his days gathered to him, making him far greater than on any single day.
A tzaddik and his opponent are a balanced match, so when the tzaddik leaves the world his opponent leaves too or loses his strength: Nimrod with Avraham, Esav with Yaakov.
Vayigdelu hane'arim refers to the fifteenth birthday, when Yaakov absorbed the kedusha at Avraham's passing and Esav the tumah at Nimrod's killing.
Yitzchak loved Esav more because the food Esav brought was secretly prepared by Rivka with kedusha, so Yitzchak felt kedusha in it and took Esav for a hidden tzaddik.
Contradictory statements of the Midrash and the Zohar about the Avos can both be true, because pshat, drush and sod sometimes judge the same act differently.
Yaakov's bowing to Esav was clever according to the Zohar: it made Esav swell with pride, and that was his downfall.
Avraham's going down to Mitzrayim brought the galus, yet the galus was what purified his children, so he knowingly accepted the harm for the greater benefit.
A prophecy can still change, but a symbolic act of the Avos fixes the outcome; so Avraham took Pharaoh's money to secure that his children would leave Mitzrayim with wealth.
A gift from a rasha carries his character and tumah, which is why Avraham refused Sodom's money, while the wealth of Mitzrayim was purified by Hashem.
Yosef said 'my bones' not because he feared decay but to point to the part of him that came from his father, so the request was about Yaakov, not himself.
A son's inheritance is not ordinary inheritance by a relative: he inherits because he is the father's own continuation, and that continuation lies in the bones he received from him.
The bones endure because they are white and carry the quality of chesed from the father, while the red flesh and blood carry din from the mother and decompose.

Closeness to Yaakov comes in levels: Yaakov could not bear even temporary burial in Mitzrayim, Yosef, one level removed, could wait for the geulah, and later generations will be brought up only when Moshiach comes.
Rebbi did not curse Nebuchadnezzar while teaching Yirmiyah because in learning Torah one is present at the moment described, when he was still a living king.

Since time, place and soul mirror one another, just as there is a place where Torah may not be learned there is a corresponding time, which is the night of Nittel; yet time is holier than place, so the impurity has less grip on it.
The Mashgiach reads the debate between Yitzchak and Yishmael over Milah as the first seed of the war being fought between Yishmael and the Jews today.
'Pere adam' puts the wildness as the noun and 'adam' as the description: Yishmael is wild in essence and only looks like a man, so his education or profession does not change him.
Loving chicken is really loving oneself; true essential love, like a father's for his son, does not rest on any benefit.
Avraham's first test, the fire, was self-sacrifice for his life's ideal; the Akedah demanded sacrificing that very ideal, which is why without it the other tests would lack their value.
Milah at eight days and the Akedah are one idea: a Jew's bond to Hashem does not need understanding, so an infant's Milah is equal to an adult's.
Recalling the Bris and the Akedah when asking for mercy asks Hashem to respond from a bond beyond reason, even when Jews do not deserve it.

Avraham's mention of Eliezer, who drew from his Torah and gave it to others, is part of his complaint: he already had a spiritual child to spread Hashem's name, but what he lacked was a biological child, since good midos pass only through the body.

Following the Derashos HaRan, the word 'na' made the Akeidah a request Avraham could have declined; since a tzaddik prays when a decree falls on others, he could have prayed for the sake of Klal Yisrael's midos.

Avraham's loss of his madreigos and his seeing the place 'from afar' at the Akeidah is the pattern of the hester panim of the last generation before Moshiach, so his conduct then would be duplicated in his children's last test.

The Akeidah stood at the three beginnings: Avraham the beginning of the souls of Yisrael, Har HaMoriah the beginning of place, and Yom Kippur, which Yechezkel calls Rosh Hashanah, the beginning of time; from there it reaches the furthest place, the last time and the last souls.
The words 'asher ahavta' did not just describe Avraham's love; they created in him a love for Yitzchak above natural parental love, and that created love is what he had to set aside.
Avraham chose emunah over midos, and when Yitzchak was spared he was granted both, which is why Jews today are both merciful, modest and kind and believers the children of believers.
Hashem's affectionate 'Avraham, Avraham' is heard today by every Jew with mesiras nefesh for Torah, emunah and chinuch, as heirs of Avraham's test.

The halacha that a raiser counts as a parent was hidden even from Yaakov by design: had it been known, Eshes Potiphar would have sent Asnas to Yosef, and Yosef would never have had the tests that made him a tzaddik.
A title like tzaddik is earned only through tests; Yosef's brothers were also holy, but without tests they did not earn the name.
Eshes Potiphar sought Moshiach ben Yosef just as Tamar sought Moshiach ben David, which is a further reason the two parshiyos stand side by side.

Yishmael's milah, being surgery rather than a bris, is empty, so they were given Eretz Yisrael only while it is empty; as the land fills with Jews they sense their end and resist like a candle flaring before it dies.
The Avos could read the Torah from the world, as an architect can read the blueprint from a finished building.
Melech Yavan equals Yosef in gematria (156), showing that the war of Chanukah was a battle of the holiness of Yosef.

The names of the chief of evil, without the divine letters that sustain him, together with his mate Lilis, equal 580, the count of Yaakov's gift; so the gift is like the Yom Kippur goat, a bone thrown to the forces of evil to leave Yaakov alone.
Unlike Eliyahu's ox, which had to be persuaded, Yaakov's animals volunteered to go to Esav, because Yaakov's level raised his animals above those of Eliyahu.

The unlearned man's chiddush concerned Esav's gift because his own letter in the Torah lay in the verses of the animals sent to Esav; that is why he was unlearned, and why this chiddush belonged to his soul.

The unlearned man's wish to be quoted was his soul's hidden plea: since repeating Torah in the speaker's name brings redemption, he sought redemption from his exile under Esav, and his public declaration that he will return itself speeds his return.
Yaakov was not faulted for failing to seek a rasha for his daughter; he owed Esav a wife because he married Leah, who was Esav's match, so Dina should have been the 581st animal of the gift.

What Esav took through Shechem he had to give back: Osnas married Yosef, who was given Shechem and buried there, and Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon came from this episode, a sign that the whole gift will return.

The Mashgiach reads 'vayifga bamakom' and 'vayifgeu bo malachei Elokim' as a reversal: leaving, Yaakov was astonished at the angels; returning after twenty years in Haran, the angels were astonished at him.
Yaakov is the choicest of the Avos not despite his earthly affairs but because of them: he showed that Hashem can dwell on a person through family, work and wealth.

The difference between olah and shelamim mirrors the difference between the nations and Yisrael: a goy may bring only an olah, wholly given to G-d, while a Jew's shelamim, eaten at a feast, shows that his own enjoyment can be holy; Klal Yisrael became a nation through the Korban Pesach, which is eaten.
Yaakov kissed and wept at once because he kissed Rachel as one kisses tefillin, seeing in her the Shechinah, and wept out of pity for the onlookers who mocked him and could not see what he saw.

The seven years seemed like days, the reverse of ordinary longing, because for Yaakov the preparation was itself avodas Hashem, just as building a sukkah is a mitzvah to be enjoyed and not only a preparation.
Yaakov's striving for Lavan's sheep, which looks like cunning on the surface, was the redemption of Jewish neshamos held captive by Lavan, who became the 600,000 Jews in Mitzrayim.

Yaakov's fourteen years in the yeshiva of Shem and Ever correspond to the preparation of Shacharis with tallis and tefillin, which readies a Jew to hallow his workday as Yaakov hallowed his work in Haran.
The Akeidah was the hardest test because it required each of the Avos to act against his own midah: Avraham of chesed had to slaughter, and Yitzchak of din had to give himself up out of love.
Hashem arranged that Yitzchak bless Yaakov thinking he was Esav, to show that Jews are blessed even when they act like Esav, and that Hashem, not Yitzchak, chooses whom to bless.
Since Torah is compared to water, the Dor HaMabul, who refused the Torah meant for them, received it as the waters of the flood, over forty days like the forty days of Matan Torah.

The Gemara's derivation of Moshe from 'beshagam hu basar' is explained by the Zohar: Noach was meant to be Moshe, and Moshe's plea 'mecheini na' repaired Noach's failure to daven for his generation, which is why the flood is called 'mei Noach'.
Lavan's sheep were a stage in the cleansing of the souls of the Dor HaMabul and Dor HaHaflagah, between the Haflagah and Mitzrayim; the Yismach Moshe remembered being one of them.

Yaakov's sticks were the mitzvah of tefillin, which recall Yetzias Mitzrayim, because extricating these souls from Lavan was itself a redemption like Yetzias Mitzrayim; it was concealed as a trick so that the Satan would not interfere.
Lavan's claim that everything Yaakov had was his, though Yaakov had brought him blessing, is the pattern of all golus: the nations prosper through the Jews and then accuse them of draining them.
A nisayon is also a raising up: like a child promoted after each exam, each test lifted Avraham higher, and the Akeidah was his final graduation.
The Akeidah was harder than Ur Kasdim not because of the sacrifice but because Avraham had to obey while Hashem seemed far away and contradictory, without the clarity he had always had.
The questions people have on Hashem have no substance; during a test the answers are hidden by Heavenly decree, and they become simple only afterward, as the Rashi on the Akeidah shows.

At the Akeidah Avraham was transported into the condition of ikvesa d'Meshicha, and 'eikev asher shamata' means he obeyed in the condition of the heel; that is why his emunah reaching the heel sustains the last generation.
Emes, the last word of Shema, corresponds to the heel; it is not written in the Sefer Torah but added by us, just as in the last generation the truth is not seen and must be believed in the dark.
Shema Yisrael, the last verse of Malchiyos, equals 'shofar shel ayil' in gematria: the shofar of the Akeidah's ram is how Klal Yisrael accepts Hashem's kingship.

The calendar year mirrors world history: as the shofar disperses the year-end clouds, the great shofar will disperse the clouds of the end of days and the world will start anew, with the strength of the ram hinted at in 'Bereishis'.
The first test, defying Nimrod for a G-d who had never spoken to him, was smaller than the Akeidah because at the Akeidah Hashem, though He spoke, was felt as far away: 'he saw the place from afar'.
At the Akeidah Avraham was brought down from all his levels to the state of the simplest Jew of the time before Moshiach, and his test was to break through from there.
The simple answer to Avraham's question, that Hashem had only said to bring Yitzchak up, was itself withheld from him; not finding the answer was part of the test.

Because Avraham's last test was a test of questions, the last generation before Moshiach will be tested with questions, and the Mashgiach places the questions raised after the Holocaust in this frame.
Giving up one's will for Hashem's is a mesiras nefesh greater than letting oneself be killed, and many small acts of it gather into a great one.
The barrenness of Avraham and Sarah was needed to break the natural continuity from father to son, so that what was born to them would be a new creation rather than an extension of Terach.
Avraham's exemption from honoring his father follows from his being a new species: kibbud av expresses a son's bond with his father, and that bond was cut.
The kofer is named for the pitch, 'kofer', that covered Noach's ark: his denial is only a coating over a belief that remains underneath.
The three matzos correspond to the Avos because grain gives intellect, which comes from the father, and the four cups to the Imahos because wine gives feeling, which comes from the mother.
Although lineage and inheritance follow the father, Jewishness follows the mother because it rests on emunah, which is transmitted through the mother.
Just as the noun drops the final nun of its root (shen, gan), 'emunah' is linked to 'em', mother, showing that emunah comes from the mother.
The Mashgiach reads the Rambam's limit as a matter of choice: a bad sign is only where a person had no choice, and only the first night of Sukkos obliges him to eat in the sukkah.
Leaving the sukkah for rain does not end one's dwelling there, just as a man's home address does not change when he steps out; therefore the exemption of one who suffers fits the mitzvah of dwelling.
An eruv is fixed for one day by placing a meal, but the sukkah must be fixed as a home for seven days, which needs an actual eating on the first night; this is why the kezayis is learned from matzah.

Tishrei is the yearly rebuilding of Chava for Adam: Rosh Hashanah as back to back, the shofar breaking through judgment, Yom Kippur as the separation, the sukkah as chuppah, and Shemini Atzeres as 'He brought her to the man'.
The Mashgiach applies the Ramban's rule, that what comes from love carries a lighter punishment, to explain why a nesuah is punished by strangling while an arusah is stoned.
The missing heh in the Torah's word for a young woman points to what she lacks until nisuin, when she receives the heh and is raised to be one with her husband.
The breaking of the luchos at the end of the Torah is joined to its first word, Bereishis, which holds everything like a seed; so a broken Sukkos becomes a new beginning.

The Mashgiach explains that the emunah of Yidden is not a sign of weak intellect, as with the fool who believes everything, but of its height: some matters are above the mind, and wise believers accept them, so that this emunah draws down wisdom.
Because time was created from the Torah and the Torah is above time, the parsha that speaks of the beginning of time is a higher court where the decrees of Rosh Hashanah can be appealed.
The Torah ends with 'Yisrael' and begins with 'Bereishis', which the Mashgiach connects to the letters of the Torah and the souls of Yisrael being one.
The greatest treasury above, of matnas chinam, is open only to one who truly feels he deserves nothing; this is how the Mashgiach reads Noach finding chen when he too was meant to be erased.
The Mashgiach explains that Avner was hinted only in the middle letters of the passuk because the erasure of a Jew can only be temporary; at his root he remains connected.
The first parsha cannot end with destruction, so it ends with 'v'Noach matza chen', a tikkun; and Noach's chen, unlike the generation of the flood's, was found in Shabbos, Torah and tefillah.

Following the Yismach Moshe, a promise made with the Name Havaya cannot be held back by sin, so the redemption must come with open miracles like Yetzias Mitzrayim, and this is the point of joining the Torah's end to Bereishis.

The Torah dwells on Eliezer's words more than on the deeds of the Avos because the Avos' greatness is beyond our understanding, while Eliezer, a smaller man, can be understood, so his awareness of hashgacha is something we can learn from.
Rivka and Lavan heard the same account of Eliezer; what each took from it reveals who they were: she was drawn to the tzaddik, he saw an easy mark for his greed.

Rivka did not take off her new bracelets to show her mother, defying the very nature on which the halachos of jewelry on Shabbos in perek Bameh Ishah are built, because she was absorbed in the tzaddik she had seen.

'Tzemidim' is written in full when Rivka receives the bracelets and without the letter yud when Lavan sees them, showing that she sensed the holiness of the bracelets that corresponded to the Luchos and he did not.
Keeping holy bracelets on is like a Jew who davened well and does not want to take off his tallis and tefillin afterwards.
The Mashgiach reads Eliezer 'standing over the camels, over the spring' as standing over his eye: his eye does not dictate to him, he decides when it may look.
Moshiach will not conquer the world with weapons but with the power of his word, the same power Avraham showed when his hesped moved the people of Ches to give him the grave.
Eliezer's negiah went unnoticed even by him until he retold the events and reflected on them; only on review did he realize he had a personal interest.
Eliezer chose kindness as the sign rather than piety or long davening, because middos pass down by inheritance while other virtues he himself also had.
The greatest success is when the force of evil itself consents to the blessing, so that it can no longer accuse; this happened when Lavan-Bilam said 'blessed of Hashem'.

Rivkah's leaving Lavan's house was a model of the Exodus: a sorcery held that none could leave, and when the moment came that she could no longer remain in impurity, she left in haste with self-sacrifice.

The Ramban's plain reading that Yitzchak went to chat with friends hints at the Kedushas Levi's idea: in a time of great accusation, a tzaddik's prayer is hidden in ordinary speech so the accusing angels let it through.
Avraham was granted Me'aras HaMachpelah measure for measure: because he ignored his own comfort for his guests, Adam and Chava had to give up their comfort for him.
Eliezer's name, read as 'my G-d is help', points to the 'ezer kenegdo', the helpmate he went to find for Yitzchak; it is left out precisely because this shidduch needed no human helper.
R' Yaakov Emden's reading of the word shadchan as 'speaks falsehood, takes money' is no joke: the shadchan is paid precisely because his lie is what lets something so holy come down into this world.

The Torah spells out Eliezer's prayers at length because the Avos served Hashem in a hidden way, while the avodah of a servant, on a lower level, is visible, so through him one sees what avodas Hashem looks like.

The bracelets Lavan saw still on Rivka's hands show that she never took them off to show them, so absorbed was she in Eliezer's avodah; Lavan read the same scene as a pious man 'above the camels' of treasure who could be exploited.
Following the Bnei Yissaschar, the word for bracelets is written with a yud when Eliezer gives them but without it when Lavan sees them, because Lavan did not see the Ten Commandments they stood for.
Avraham eulogized Sarah before negotiating for the grave so that his words of mussar would break the Bnei Ches' love of money, and they would not demand everything he had.

Sarah's first three years, before she served Hashem, were made up by her rising at night, as in 'she rises while it is still night' in Eishes Chayil; so all 127 years were equally good, and Esther merited all 127 provinces.
Greater praise of Hashem than the creation of heaven and earth is that men like Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov came into His world; this is why the first bracha calls Him the G-d of the Avos.
Terach could hand Avraham over to be killed because, as the Maharal explains, Avraham was a new creation with no true bond to his father; a father's instinctive mercy did not apply.
The Jewish body itself is different from the gentile body, like Shabbos, which outwardly looks like any weekday yet is another world.
Noach's covenant is a sign in the heavens, asking mankind to look up and forget the body; Avraham's is in the flesh, because the Jewish task is to make holiness shine in the body.
Avraham feared because the first promise of 'seed' could mean disciples, children of the soul, which Eliezer already fulfilled; so Hashem specified children 'from your innards'.
The Asher Yatzar bracha shows that the functioning of the lowest organs is spoken of before the Kisei HaKavod, so high is the Jewish body.
The Sanhedrin needs dayanim of yichus and fathers of children because mercy in judgment is a bodily middah passed down from the Avos.
The Mashgiach reads lech lecha as 'go to yourself': to one's own soul and root, since everything around a person is only a garment of this world; the same words open and close Avraham's trials.
Lot, who tagged along with Avraham, represents Avraham's bad side: even when a servant of Hashem leaves the wicked, a part of the bad drags along with him.
Avraham was not made the first Jew because he was a tzaddik; rather, the world needed a first Jew, and he is a tzaddik because he is the root of all the tzaddikim of Klal Yisrael.

Canaan was given Eretz Yisrael precisely because he was cursed to be a servant: a servant can hold his master's land until the master comes, and the Mashgiach applies the same reasoning to Yishmael, son of Hagar, Sarah's maidservant.
Og was named after the matzos because his report, though meant for evil, saved the sparks of Moshiach in Lot's family, and matzah carries the power of every redemption.

Og's height of nine amos and width of four amos correspond, according to the Mashgiach, to the letters of Hashem's Name, showing how high he reached and therefore how great a kiddush Hashem his downfall was.
Chazal knew that the service of the heart is tefillah because man is a small world: his heart corresponds to Yerushalayim, and Yerushalayim is the house of prayer.
As Yerushalayim is the heart of the world, the blessing of the avos is the heart of tefillah and of the Jewish people, which is why it alone requires kavanah.
The Torah hides Avraham's righteousness, as it first leaves Moshe's parents unnamed, to show that the Jewish people's existence did not depend on any individual's merit.
The Ramban's charge that Avraham sinned is itself praise: he was chosen despite a sin at the very start of his story, since a Jew's sin is only incidental.
Korbanos and teshuvah help a Jew because his sin is like dirt that washes off, while in a non-Jew a sin is part of his essence; this is how the korbanos answer Avraham's question 'how will I know'.
Rebbi did not curse Nebuchadnezzar when learning Yirmiyahu because Torah study carries the learner into the time of the text, when Nebuchadnezzar was still a reigning king.

The animals saved in the ark were those under Noach's share of creation: since each person's part of the world follows his deeds, Noach's righteousness kept his part pure, and Eretz Yisrael, also his share, was not flooded.
The Torah differs from other history books in that it tells not what happened but what is going to happen, so the fulfillment of its prophecies proves the coming of the end as well.

The Torah deliberately hides the merits behind the great turning points, Moshe's parents and Avraham's self-sacrifice in Ur Kasdim, so that no one should think the Jewish people came about by chance merit; it had to come from somewhere regardless.
The Ramban opens Avraham's story with his sin precisely to stress that Avraham's coming did not depend on his merits; the purpose of creation required him.

The war of the four kings was a war against Moshiach: they captured Lot because Moshiach was to descend from him, and Avraham's victory over them foreshadows the Jews passing successfully through the four exiles.
Esav's kiss was another form of his bite, and the exile of Edom, after failing to destroy the Jews by force, succeeds more by embracing them.

The flood and Matan Torah were the same downpour: the nations rightly sensed the signs of the flood at Sinai, but what came in Noach's time as the outer shell, destruction, came at Sinai as its inner content, Torah.
Moshe's 'erase me' on behalf of his generation repaired Noach's failure to daven for his; the flood is called 'the waters of Noach' because of that failure.
The shin on the head tefillin, three-headed and four-headed and numbering 300, expresses the threefold quality of Torah that makes it lasting, the opposite of the flood.
The sukkah is an embassy of heaven on earth: one who sits in it is legally 'not in this world', so judgment against the world cannot reach him, just as tumah cannot remain in a mikveh.
The mazalos stopped during the flood because a single bright day whose mazal brings kindness could have broken a decree of destruction for a fixed time.

Moshe's teiva and Noach's teiva are one theme: the first gilgul was saved from the flood by a teiva, the second by a teiva and the daughter of Pharaoh, who corresponds to the 'bas malka' present in every word of Torah and tefillah.

Hashem's praise of Noach was not a compliment but chizuk: Hashem judges a person against what he could have been without his generation's obstacles, so Noach, who felt small beside earlier generations, was told he is a tzaddik in this generation.
The two readings of "in his generations", for praise and for discredit, say the same thing; the discredit is not Noach's but his generation's, which kept him from reaching Avraham's level.
The form of the word "Nefilim", like "mazik" or "chasid", describes one who not only falls but makes others fall, which is how the angels who fell polluted the atmosphere of the flood generation.
The lulav's na'anuim draw down Hashem's Name and bring it back to the chest, teaching that the knowledge of Hashem's presence must move from the mind into the heart so it remains after Sukkos.
One attached to Torah carries the sukkah within himself all year, as the Yismach Moshe was told that Gan Eden is in the Tanna; this is the inner meaning of Marcheshvan.

The raven's refusal was a lesson to Noach: it was reserved for Eliyahu, the herald of redemption, so one must wait for Hashem to send the salvation, just as the Jews did not flee Egypt during the darkness.
Unlike Avraham, who needed no support and was praised for humility, today's generation needs chizuk, so each Jew must hear "ki oscha ra'isi tzaddik" as said to him.
The Mashgiach reads 'mecheini' as containing 'mei Noach': Moshe's readiness to be erased for Klal Yisrael was the tikkun of the waters named for Noach.
Mesiras nefesh for a generation means including oneself in it, saying 'I am one of them'; this is why Moshe broke the luchos, to declare that he too had sinned.
Avraham was not permitted mesiras nefesh in Canaan because Hashem's promise of a great nation depended on him, so Hashem revealed Sodom's fate to him in order that he pray instead.
Kayin's 'Am I my brother's keeper?' is read as true words of teshuvah: Hashem, who created the yetzer hara, is the only true guard against it.
The Gemara learns 'adam hamazik' from a verse about asking and repenting, because man's defining trait as a damager is his ability to make a tikkun.
An owner's liability for his ox reflects that his property extends his soul: the goring comes from his own middos, not from heaven.
The same 'inclination of man's heart is evil' that justified the flood became, after Noach's admission of helplessness, the ground for Hashem's promise never to flood the world again.

The Mashgiach locates the Flood generation's worst sin not in committing evil but in legalizing it: when sin becomes written law and culture, people no longer feel shame, which is far worse than a private yetzer hara.

The animals that entered the ark and Eretz Yisrael were spared because they were Noach's portion of creation, which did not sin since he did not; Noach is Shabbos, and Eretz Yisrael is the 'Shabbos' of the lands.

The forty days and nights of the Flood's rain were the outer form of the Torah that was due to descend in Noach's time; at Matan Torah, under the same heavenly configuration, the same forty days brought down its inner treasure instead.

Moshe Rabbeinu was a reincarnation of Noach: Noach's failure to pray for his generation, for which the Flood is called 'mei Noach', was repaired when Moshe said 'erase me from Your book' for his people.

The teivah is the sukkah of Parshas Noach: just as a sukkah protects not by its wood but by the halachos that are names of Hashem, the ark's measurements are themselves Hashem's name, so learning the parsha extends Tishrei's protection.

Shimon HaTzaddik, as the last of the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, told a frightened generation that the world does not stand on the Knesses HaGedolah but on Torah, avodah and gemilus chasadim; the Mashgiach applies this to a generation left without its great tzaddikim.

Following the Ba'al Shem Tov as explained by Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, 'tzohar ta'aseh lateivah' means: make each word of Torah and tefillah luminous, for today's world is a flood and only a lit-up 'teivah' saves.

The Mashgiach explains that decay entered the world through the sin of the Tree of Knowledge, a breach of bris, so wherever bris is kept nothing spoils: the ark's food, Yosef's grain, the bodies of tzaddikim.
According to the Mashgiach, every person owns a portion of creation that his sins spoil; Noach's animals and his land, Eretz Yisrael, had not sinned, which is why the flood did not fall there.
The Mashgiach holds that the lion in the ark ate straw as in the world of tikkun, so Noach brought no meat at all, and the Ibn Ezra's question about carnivores never arises.
The Mashgiach explains the lion's blow: after Cham's sin the lion suddenly needed meat, Noach had none, the straw came too late, and Hashem no longer made miracles for creatures that had sinned.

He reads the two descriptions of Noach as two moments: 'tzaddik in this generation' is Hashem's word before the flood, when the world was to restart from Noach, while 'tzaddik tamim in his generations', written later by Moshe, points to Avraham.
The Mashgiach sees Tishrei as a Jew's personal world of tikkun and Cheshvan as its flood, and following the Ba'al Shem Tov, the ark he must enter is the words of Torah and tefillah.
He points out that the same evil inclination that brought the flood became the reason for the promise of no more flood, showing a Jew's power to turn things around.
The 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu, read before Rosh Hashanah, match the 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah, and each parsha's count matches one stage of teshuvah.

The Mabul was the 'envelope' of Torah without its contents; Matan Torah was the same flood returning with its inner Torah, which is why the nations feared a Mabul, and 'oz' is linked to 'mabul' by gematria.
Noach was 'mi'ketanei amanah' because at first the rain was gishmei brachah with Torah inside it, and he saw that Torah; only later did it become an empty mabul.
Building the teivah for 120 years was itself the way Noach drew teshuvah into the world, since the teivah, like a sukkah and a mikveh, is built of holy names and comes from Binah.
Those in the teivah did not want to leave because they felt its holiness, like the 'people of the sukkah', which is why Hashem had to tell Noach 'go out of the teivah'.
The world's autumn, the month called 'Bul' from 'mabul', when everything withers, is the spring of Klal Yisroel, since Parshas Noach ends with the birth of Avraham Avinu.

The lion's attack on Noach was not a lapse in Hashem's help but the result of Cham's sin: once the ark's world was damaged, Hashem no longer gave special help to its sinful inhabitants, and the flaw reached Noach himself.
Noach's drinking was a mistake about the time: he thought the world of the ark was already the renewed world, when wine may be drunk freely, as it will be when Eliyahu comes.

Bilaam's answer at Matan Torah means that the Torah was the inner content of the flood: the same flood that came down as empty water in Noach's time came down at Sinai as Torah, a 'mabul' with a shin, hinted in 'bashalom'.
The halachic measurements of the ark, like those of the sukkah, are what make it a vessel for the holy names that place it outside this world, so that judgment cannot reach whoever is inside.
Bar Daroma could have been Moshiach, and his failure came from the generation's reliance on his strength; the snake that killed him is the power that makes Jews forget that Hashem runs the world.
Noach was reborn as Moshe: having failed to daven for his generation, as Moshe he gave himself for Klal Yisrael and gave the Torah that the generation of the flood was meant to receive.

Eating is not only for strength to serve Hashem: every moment brings a new heavenly influence, and food is one of the channels through which a person takes in that new holiness; this is why the righteous will eat the Leviasan feast before a new order begins.
Yitzchak loved Esav for a real holiness he tasted, but it was Yaakov's: Yaakov secretly prepared the food Esav served, so Yitzchak concluded that Esav was a hidden tzaddik greater than Yaakov.

"Ki tzayid befiv" is the Torah's way of recording what happened without writing a falsehood: it was Esav's hunt only in his mouth, by his claim, while the extra hei in "tzeidah", written but not read, hints that Yaakov did the slaughtering.

The blessing of the dew of heaven and the fat of the land came measure for measure: because Yaakov's food was full of holiness, he was blessed with food whose inner side is holiness and which brings Torah.
Yitzchak left Rechovos precisely when he finally had peace, because comfort itself told him he was not in the place a person is sent to this world for.

Following the Yaaros Devash, the Mashgiach explains that asking to be a seal on Hashem's heart was not proper, since a heart is sometimes open and sometimes closed; the hands, one's deeds, are always revealed, and that is where a Jew is measured.

According to the Yismach Moshe, Yaakov and Esav were born together so that each would have free choice through contact with the other, and Yaakov received the blessing in Esav's clothes to show that even then a Jew merits blessing.
Yitzchak's love of 'game in his mouth' was not appetite: he loved Eisav because he felt kedushah in the food he served, and the food was in truth cooked by Rivkah.
Rashi's two readings of 'game in his mouth' are both true and need each other: Eisav brought him food, and with that same food he deceived him into thinking he was a hidden tzaddik.
The spelling of 'tzayid' hides and reveals: the missing vav shows it was not Eisav's game, and the extra heh hints it was Rivkah's, kept as a secret from Yitzchak as it happened.

Yitzchak blessed Yaakov measure for measure: food that had brought him Torah became a blessing of food from Eretz Yisroel that brings Mikra, Mishnah, halachah and aggadah, which is the deep plain meaning, not a drash against it.
Yishmael, the kelipah of chesed (water), now holds the world's 'fire', which belongs to Yitzchak's attribute of gevurah; his fall means handing that fire back to Yitzchak.
The Torah records Yishmael's years only so Yaakov's hidden years in the yeshivah of Shem and Ever can be counted, hinting that Yishmael's fall comes through that hidden learning.

The Mashgiach reads the Greeks' breaching of the Temple walls as an attempt to add to a domain that was not theirs, the mirror image of Chanukah's increase in kedushah that reaches even the public domain below ten tefachim.
The letter yud stretched becomes a vav and stretched further a nun, so the very name Yavan alludes to Greece's drive to expand.
Yitzchak's 'matamim as I love' were not tasty food; what he tasted and loved was the kedushah the preparer put into it.
Yitzchak tasted kedushah in the food Esav served, prepared secretly by Rivka, and concluded that Esav was a hidden tzaddik, who is greater than a revealed one.
'Ki tzayid befiv' is read as Esav's deception: he brought his father food that he had not prepared himself.
Yaakov's 'kayom' means 'by your view of today': since Esav lives for today's pleasure and expects to die, by his own logic the bechorah is worthless to him.
The Mashgiach reads the Rebbe of Lublin's praise of a man who harmed his town as a glimpse of the hidden good in him, the same hidden light that the Chanukah lights reveal.
Since every power of kedusha has its counterpart in the sitra achra, the side of holiness that fights the sitra achra must itself carry the number eleven, which is why the ketores has eleven spices.
Yosef's second dream is called 'another dream' because it is not a repetition of the first but a dream of a different kind: a dream of Chanukah and the hidden light.

Chanukah's light is bound to the number nine: it appears in Kislev, the ninth month, during Vayeshev, the ninth sedra, through its ninth verse and Yosef, the ninth sefirah, all echoing the letter tes whose good is hidden inside.

Yosef, the hidden soul whose brothers did not recognize him and whose name Tzafnas means hidden, carries the power of Chanukah, and the Shelah's gematria of Yosef as 'king of Yavan' shows that he is the one who fights Yavan.

The Mashgiach resolves the age difficulty in 'vayigdelu' by reading the growth not as a matter of years but of an event: each brother became 'great' by witnessing a passing on the same day, Yaakov Avraham's and Esav Nimrod's.

Just as a tzaddik's lifetime of good deeds gathers on his last day, so the evil deeds of a rasha like Nimrod gathered at his death, drawing a convention of dark forces that left an atmosphere of impurity.
Eliyahu could give Elisha more than he himself had only because on the day of his passing all his days were gathered together.
Learning a parsha is presence, not history: because Rebbi was 'in' the time of Divrei Hayamim while learning it, he would not curse a living king there, though Nebuchadnezzar had long died.
Eliezer's gift of garments to Rivka was, according to the Shinever Rav, not for wearing but a sample showing the difference between modest and immodest clothing.
Yosef's word 'asher' in 'asher mechartem' is read, as with Moshe's 'asher shibarta', as a 'yasher koach': he thanked his brothers because being sold made him Yosef HaTzaddik.

The Mashgiach reads the absence of a break before Vayechi as a hint to Rebbi: the white space of the Torah is the Oral Torah, which should not be written, and Rebbi, a gilgul of Yaakov, filled it only because of the troubles of exile.

The Mashgiach turns the Midrash's 'all troubles were closed from him' into a stance: through bitachon a Jew in exile knows Hashem is with him, so the troubles are closed off from him even while they exist.

Shabbos, in the Lechovitcher's parable, is the inn where the frozen traveler warms up to continue; Hashem did not send the soul down for Shabbos, which it already had beneath the Throne of Glory, but for the weekdays.

From Rashi's 'the hearts of Yisrael were closed, so the parsha is closed' the Mashgiach learns that a Jew does not only relate to the Torah but affects it: when his heart is closed, the Torah itself becomes closed.
Yaakov, a man of truth, did reveal the end: the very closing of the hearts is the sign, since Moshiach will come in the darkest time, when even many Jews forget him.

The Mashgiach sees hashgachah in the yeshivos learning Yevamos during Shovavim: a masechta about yibum, bringing back a soul that did not complete its task, is itself a tikkun hanefesh, and that is why it is hard.

Praise of Hashem requires kedushah: the ofanim rise to the level of the seraphim by saying 'kadosh', and so the order of praise in Shemoneh Esrei ends with HaKel HaKadosh, the bracha set against Yaakov.

The white parchment around the letters of a Sefer Torah is the Oral Torah; the missing space before Vayechi, a closed parsha, is where Rebbe 'wrote what should not be written', and that is his hint in the Torah.
Rebbe opened the Mishnah with Shema at night, the words the Shevatim said to Yaakov, continuing Yaakov's acceptance of Heaven's yoke in the night of exile.

The day of Yosef's climactic test was the Egyptians' festival, identified in a sefer as Nittel; on the most impure day he became the holiest Jew, showing that growth comes davka where the air is impure.

Since a person's bones come from his father, Yosef's bones are Yaakov's continuation, so bringing them up completes Yaakov's burial; this explains why he told his brothers rather than his sons, and why all the tribes' bones were taken.
Kiryas Sefer is both a real city and the three thousand halachos, because each part of Eretz Yisrael has Torah written upon it; whoever restored those halachos held the key to that territory.
Because the Jews are the Torah itself, their spiritual state is mirrored in the very layout of the Torah: the closing of their hearts in Egypt shows up as a closed parsha.
Yaakov read in the absence of ches and tes from the tribes' names that knowing the end is not part of a Jew's mission, since each name hints at its bearer's mission.
Covering the shofar until it is blown, the matzah at the Seder and the challos, and the hidden lineage of Moshiach, all follow one rule: the greatest good is hidden so the Satan should not accuse.

The two opinions on the pilegesh of Givah are both true: the husband did not mind the fly, but the hair revealed that she lacked the traits of Jewish daughters, turning the fly in hindsight into negligence.
The punishment for not protesting Michah's idol waited until Givah, because only when the Jews fought for a person's honor did it become clear that they could have fought for Hashem's.
The widow's laxness about uncovered water is a hint to Knesses Yisrael in galus: without 'the fear of the husband' she is exposed to the snake's poison.
The missing space of nine letters before Vayechi is filled by the words 'Vayechi Yaakov': where the closing is, there one finds that Yaakov lives.
Read as 'vey geshrien', the word Vayigash itself is the cry of woe of the Midrash, the fear of the day of judgment and rebuke.

The brothers' terror was not fear of punishment but the shock of seeing Yosef's concealed holiness, the inner point of the bris hidden under the orlah of Egyptian garments; the shame of the future will be the same discovery about the whole world.
The same wagons that carried Yaakov into galus hint to the 'tzabim' in which the nations will bring the Jews back, for the geulah is hinted in the very place of the galus.
Yaakov's refusal to be consoled proves he knew Yosef was alive, since one is consoled only over the dead; his grief was fear for Yosef's spiritual life.
A wheel, which turns around one point that itself does not turn, was Yosef's message that everything revolves around the inner point of Yesod, and that this point in him had held firm.
Since people avoid the number connected with their failing, Yosef's choosing to send six wagons, the number of his middah, was proof that he had not fallen in it.
The departure of Shabbos Vayigash, leading into Asarah b'Teves, is itself a levayah, as Yaakov escorted Yosef and as Hashem promised to go down with Yaakov.

The Mashgiach links three generations as one group of souls: the builders of the Tower who wanted 'a name' became Sedom, and the survivors of Tzoar became Korach's 'anshei shem', each return carrying the unpaid account of the last.
Through the Chasam Sofer, 'G-d of all flesh' is read as G-d of the body and not only of the soul: a reincarnated soul's sin is not a reason to make the new, innocent body suffer.

The Mashgiach distinguishes repairing a blemish from being punished for it: a tzaddik or baal teshuvah may still need to mend an old pegam, yet he is a new person before Hashem and his body does not suffer for the old sin.

'Elokei Avraham' is itself the malchus of the first bracha of Shemoneh Esrei, which does not say 'Melech ha'olam', because Hashem's kingship is shown by His having a tzaddik like Avraham in the world.

Avraham's chesed was mesirus nefesh precisely because it went to those he had most reason to reject: he, who understood better than anyone how to despise idolatry, served idolaters, and he prayed for Sedom, who would have lynched him.
Following the Lubliner Rav, Onkelos's rendering of Avraham's words to Sarah came from his own life: as a convert he felt, as Avraham did, the chesed of being taken out of idolatry.

The Akeidah and Yishmael's expulsion are one test: Avraham, the embodiment of chesed, had to act with gevurah against his own nature, and according to the Ran he did so when it was only a request, not a command.

Rebbi cursed Nevuchadnetzar only when reading the Megillah and not while learning a passage where he was alive, showing that learning Torah places a person in the very time of the events, not in a history book.
Each year's shofar thins the partition holding back Moshiach, so even after thousands of years the Satan is more frightened than before (in the name of the Satmar Rav).
Moshiach's root is hidden in the most shameful origin, Moav, born of Lot's daughters, so that the forces of impurity should never think to look for it there.

The successive sealings, Yom Kippur, Hoshana Rabbah and Chanukah, were revealed one after another as the generations weakened: fasting for the great, joy for the weaker, and simple routine for the generation of ikvesa d'meshicha.
The first quarter of the year, from 25 Elul to 25 Kislev, is like infancy that does not yet count, and likewise a person's first twenty years are his time before the seal.
'He saw the place from afar' means Avraham went to the Akeidah without feeling, and this last test of Avraham corresponds to the last generation before Moshiach, which serves without emotion.

The Mashgiach reads the Ba'al Shem Tov as saying that immorality is the finest middah, chesed, the very middah with which Hashem created the world, spent on base things; this is why the Torah calls it 'chesed'.

The right tefillin strap is longer than the left because din must be shorter and chesed dominant, and even a sofer writing right to left draws the base of a letter from left to right, mixing in some din.

The Jewish leap year, which aligns the lunar year with the solar seasons, expresses the blend of chesed (the white moon) with din (the red sun), while the Arabs' purely lunar calendar reflects unblended chesed.
Yitzchak, pure din, never has a sidra alone, while Bereishis opens with Avraham alone and ends with Yaakov alone, since pure din is not allowed to stand by itself.

Sodom's condemnation lay in combining opposite extremes: cruelty alone could be excused as a nature of din and immorality alone as an excess of love, but both together reveal a deliberate rebellion against Hashem.

Since Eretz Yisrael is tied to the 'bris esh' of milah and esh is the first of the four elements, giving the land to Yishmael also gave his descendants the element of fire, energy, which the Mashgiach sees in their control of the world's oil.
Yishmael's expulsion comes immediately after Yitzchak's milah: once a true milah appears, the imitation is darkened, a sign for the future of Yishmael's hold on the land.
The word nisayon is read as raising up: a test is like a child's exam for promotion, and the tenth test was Avraham's 'graduation'.
For a prophet who sees Hashem, obeying is easy; the real test was a command that seemed to contradict Hashem's own promise.
The answer to Avraham's question was so simple a child could give it; the point of a test is that the answer is hidden, and when Moshiach comes history's questions will have equally simple answers.
The last generation corresponds to the heels of Adam's body: just as a prick in the heel is hardly felt, these souls barely feel Hashem, and that is why emunah is their test.
Avraham's mesirus nefesh at the Akeidah went against his own life's ideal, and so proved retroactively that his nine earlier sacrifices were not for an ideal or for honor.
Small acts of going beyond one's habit each count as a little mesirus nefesh, and they add up to a great sum, the Jewish answer to Yishmael's boasting of self-sacrifice.
The Mashgiach reads 'passim' as 'pas yam': the coat declared Yosef the tzaddik for whom the sea would split, and that, not favoritism, is what alarmed the brothers.
Rachel's silence when Leah was brought to the chupah is a form of guarding the bris, since guarding speech and guarding the bris are one, and this is why her son became the provider of the world.
The law that raising an orphan makes one a parent was hidden even from Yaakov until Yosef passed his test, and then it was learned specifically from a passuk about Yosef.
Yosef's request 'remember me' really meant 'do not remember me unless you need me': he preferred two more years in prison to a geulah owed to a human favor.
In the dream, Yaakov and Rachel bowing to the ground hint at Hakadosh Baruch Hu and the Shechinah descending to the earth, and Yaakov's outcry was a cry over the length of the galus.
The cupbearer's dream, with its fourfold 'kos', was a dream of Yosef's and Klal Yisrael's geulah, so its interpretation as release came true, while the baker's was a dream of galus.

The greater the light, the more deeply it must be hidden: Hashem hid the light of Moshiach inside the most troubling stories of Vayeshev, as one hides a diamond in a garbage can where no thief would look.

The parsha moves from questions on the Shevatim to Yosef being imprisoned for his righteousness, mirroring the Rambam's point that speaking against tzaddikim leads to speaking against Hashem; this makes Vayeshev a drill in emunah.
Because the Torah is the soul of Klal Yisrael, its scattered halachos reflect the people's exile, and the many collections of seforim in our time reflect the beginning of their ingathering.
Yosef supported Yaakov for seventeen years to repay the seventeen years Yaakov supported him, because Yosef's nature is to be a giver, not a receiver.
Just as the world and the calendar have the structure of a body, Mitzrayim is the lowest land and Nittel the lowest day, and Yosef won his greatest perfection precisely in that place and on that day.

Nitzavim, Vayelech and Ha'azinu together have 122 pesukim, matching the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah, and the last passuk, about seeing the land from afar without entering, matches the Chanukah lights, which may be looked at but not used.
Chanukah's date is fixed by neither Shabbos nor Rosh Chodesh but by the number eight, which is above time, so on Chanukah a Jew can still complete what belongs to Rosh Hashanah.

Yosef credits his mother's silence rather than her greater active deed because his kingship and power to sustain others came from shmiras habris, and her silence, not shaming Leah, was a guarding of the bris of the mouth.

The halacha that raising an orphan makes one a parent was withheld from Yaakov and Potiphar's wife on purpose: had it been known, Yosef would have married Osnas without the trial that raised him to the level of the Avos; it was revealed retroactively, and its root in the Torah is Yosef's own dream.

Because the Satan fears Moshiach, the line of David is hidden in unlikely places like Lot's daughters and Moav, as a diamond is hidden in a garbage can, and the halacha permitting a Moabite woman was revealed only when needed.
Yavan opposed chodesh, Shabbos and milah because each is a havdalah, and creation itself is built of havdalos; Chanukah answers measure for measure by bringing light into the darkest nights.

The letters of Yosef's name hint at his role: yud and vav are the giving letters of Hashem's name, and samech and pei hint at sixty masechtos and eighty braisos, which is why the kesones 'passim' carried the same samech and pei.
Osnas held to kedushah alone in Egypt because she saw Yosef's conduct and drew from his example; like the Chanukah light, Yosef brings light into the very place of darkness.

The Mashgiach reads Yaakov's ignorance of a simple Gemara as deliberate concealment from Above: the law had to stay hidden so that Yosef would face his trials and earn kingship, and it was revealed only once he became king.
Potiphar's wife was right in her astrology, since Asenath, whom she raised, truly counts as her daughter; her error came only from not knowing that chiddush.

The brothers' retort 'will you reign over us' meant that one who speaks lashon hara has broken the bris of the tongue and cannot be king; Yosef answered that he would reign in the merit of his mother's silence.

Yosef as the hidden light was placed specifically in Egypt, the reshus harabim and place of the other side, just as the Chanukah light is placed facing the public domain, low, on the left and in the darkest nights.

Asenath's name comes from the thornbush (sneh): like Hashem in the thornbush and like Yosef, she remained noble and holy in Egypt, which matched her to Yosef, blessed by 'the One who dwells in the thornbush'.
The Chanukah lights can kindle souls that even Shabbos cannot, the 'inferior oils', because the Chanukah light was made to shine into places that are otherwise unfit.

Even the greatest soul cannot attain on its own a portion of Torah that belongs to another living tzaddik; such a level passes on only when its holder leaves the world, as the Ba'al Shem Tov received a level when the Or HaChaim passed away.
Yaakov's Torah from Shem and Ever and Yosef's own Taharos are two kinds of Torah: what is received through the chain of tradition, and the portion that is the root of one's own soul.
Seder Taharos, the sixth order and the order learned on the sixth day, belongs to Yosef, whose trials of holiness earned him that level from heaven.
One does not say Avraham the tzaddik or Yitzchak the tzaddik, only Yosef the tzaddik: this title is Yosef's new contribution, not inherited from Yaakov.
The Chanukah flame is the level of Yosef, as the passuk calls the house of Yosef a flame, which ties Yosef's holiness to the lights of Chanukah.

The Midrash's criticism of Yaakov and Chazal's lesson from him are not a contradiction but two layers of Torah, drash and sod, worn like garments one over another; they clash only because the world has not yet reached its tikkun since Adam's sin.

Rachel's merit before Hashem was not only that she gave Leah the signs, but that she understood exile and its contradictions are needed before the tikkun, and that the Jews' sins come from the state of the world rather than from their essence.
Esav's angel appeared to Yaakov as a talmid chacham, and so the final exile is that of the erev rav, who can bring proofs no one can refute; only Hashem Himself can unmask him.
The am ha'aretz could innovate the reading of 'minchah yashivu' because his own soul came from the souls sent to Esav in Yaakov's gift, and he was only temporarily in Esav's camp.
Havdalah, the separation between holy and mundane, requires a sense of smell; so too the tzaddikim who could tell holy from unholy were those with a 'chush rei'ach', a sign associated with Moshiach.
Reading the names of the alufim of Esav brings Esav back to his root in the Torah, where he has no existence of his own, and so nullifies his power; this is a preparation for Chanukah.
Yaakov's eight bowings to Esav are not a weakness that brought on the eight kings of Edom as a punishment; they are the path of 'diminution after diminution', which in the end leads to increase.
Lavan's flocks were Jewish souls who had lost their tzelem Elokim through earlier generations' sins, and Yaakov's years of shepherding were the work of restoring their human form.
The Midrash reads 'shifchah' as Avigail because the same force in her soul that stopped David from killing Naval, Lavan reborn, is what held Yaakov back from fighting Lavan.
The touch on Yaakov's thigh, the Jews killed for kiddush Hashem, is not Esav's victory but the opposite: these loftiest souls will bring about Esav's downfall.
Shabbos requires a person to rise to Hashem, but on Chanukah Hashem comes down, just as the Mikdash came to Yaakov because the souls he carried could not rise to it.
The eighth king, Hadar, of whom no death is written, is the tikkun, and he corresponds to the eight days of Chanukah and to the time of Moshiach.
The oil Yaakov poured on the stone at Beis El was the very cruse of oil the Chashmonaim later found, so the light of Chanukah was revealed already then.

The Mashgiach reads the angels' error in Sodom through the Arizal on Egypt: a place of extreme impurity can damage even Gavriel and Rafael, and from this he shows the power of a bad environment and bad company.
The angels expelled after Sodom waited for a tzaddik who could enter a place of impurity unharmed; this explains why they were restored only when Yaakov came, after Shem and Ever and Lavan.
'Vayifga' is reversed: on the way to Charan Yaakov had the surprise of meeting the angels, but on the way back it was the angels' joy to meet Yaakov, who had redeemed them.
Yaakov sent to Esav precisely the angels who had once fallen in an impure place, because only they could testify from experience that he had lived with Lavan without being harmed.

The two nearly identical Kabbalas Shabbos psalms describe two kinds of redemption: one of din, in the way of Tishrei, judged 'bemeisharim', and one of chesed, in the way of Nissan, earned by a generation that keeps hoping 'ki va, ki va' with emunah.
The 'chamor' on which Moshiach rides is the physical, toiling Jew whose davening is hard; the greater his spark of Moshiach, the harder his prayer, and Moshiach comes through such groaning prayers.

Yaakov's demand that the angel of Esav concede the blessings is the same as the bad angel answering amen on Friday night: the completeness of the redemption is when even the side of evil must acknowledge the good.
The angels of Sedom were not punished only for the words 'ki mashchisim anachnu'; entering the tumah of Sedom itself blemished them, as the Arizal explains about Mitzrayim.
The Mashgiach suggests that 'k'eretz Mitzrayim' in the passuk about Sedom is not praise of its fertility but a statement that it was as impure as Mitzrayim.
Only a tzaddik who had himself lived in a place of tumah without being blemished could repair the blemished angels, which is why they waited until Yaakov.

Yaakov went to Shem and Ever rather than staying with Yitzchak because Yitzchak learned in a sheltered holy place, while Shem and Ever, living among goyim, taught how to serve Hashem in such surroundings.
Lavan switched the sisters as a plan to kill Yaakov: a man married to someone else's zivug must eventually divorce or die, and he knew Yaakov would not divorce Leah.
Tears can change what even tefillah cannot: as Eisav's tears opened the gates of brachah, Leah's tears changed her very root from Eisav to Yaakov.
Vayetzei is the only sedra written as one continuous parsha with no break, because Yaakov never had a moment's interruption from the way of his father's house during twenty years in Charan.
Be'er Sheva is read as the oath (shevuah): like a man lowering himself into a deep pit tied by a strong rope to the top, Yaakov could enter Charan only because his oath bound him to Hashem.
Rachel and Leah correspond to the two aspects of the Shechinah mourned in Tikkun Rachel and Tikkun Leah, which is why Yaakov had to prepare seven years for each, like counting seven times seven.
Hashem answered every request in Yaakov's vow except bread and clothing; the silence itself is the answer: rely on Me, I have not forsaken you until now.
Yaakov's sheep were Jewish souls he raised from the level of animal to the level of speech, and every Jew still carries a point from Yaakov Avinu's shepherding.
Rachel was buried on the road so she could help her children in exile who cannot drink under gentile shepherds; this is what Yaakov saw and wept over at the well.
The Arizal delighted in the Alshich's derashah not for its depth but because Lavan himself came to listen and nodded each time the Alshich exposed one of his deceptions.
Yaakov's own galus cut a road through the wilderness: what he broke through became a path and a strength for later generations to survive their galus.

The people of Charan who accused Yaakov of immodesty were Lavan's circle, and Lavan is Bilaam, whose advice later was to corrupt Klal Yisrael through immorality; the nations parade virtue exactly where they are most sunk.
Rachel's burial outside Me'aras HaMachpelah expresses the galus of the revealed Shechinah: had Rachel been there, bound forever to Yaakov, there could have been no galus.
Kiddushin is learned from a grave purchase because that is the best sign of all: the bond of two halves of one soul outlasts even death.
Parshas Vayetzei is written without any break because Yaakov never paused, even for a moment, from his attachment while in Lavan's house.
Bnei Kedem are 'the forward people', the progressive and educated; the lowest galus, the heels, is a land of progress and higher education.
Lavan's 'nakvah secharcha' was spoken to a man he thought a fool for working seven more years; Yaakov was working for the Shechinah, not for Lavan.
The flood came in the measure of days that matched the giving of the Torah: the same waters that were to descend as Torah descended as the flood when the generation refused it.

Noach did not pray for his generation not out of indifference but because they were not bound to him: a tzaddik can pray only for those connected to him, and those who do not accept the leader even harm him.
Cheshvan, the month in which the flood fell, is the month of Torah: after binding themselves to Torah on Shemini Atzeres, Jews begin a new season and a new masechta in it.
The nations' answer 'Hashem will bless His people with peace' is read as a flood with a shin: the word 'bashalom' signals a flood of Torah, not of destruction.
Learning a new masechta with hasmadah is a direct reversal of the flood generation's words 'we do not desire knowledge of Your ways'.
Masechta Yevamos is a tikkun connected with bringing Moshiach.

The greatness of Avraham's emunah, per the Maharal, was not believing in miracles but believing against his own reasonable fear that sin might cancel the promise, simply because he saw Hashem wanted it; the Mashgiach calls this the meaning of emunah, believing where one does not understand.
The Written Torah deliberately hides Avraham's mesiras nefesh and gives no reason for 'Lech lecha', so that no one should think a Jew's chosenness was earned; a Jew is a Jew 'without any reason'.

The Ramban's harsh 'great sin' is itself a praise of Avraham: precisely in the first account of the first Jew the Torah shows a sin, to teach that a Jew's sin is external and never touches his inner self.
Emunah is the opposite of subjugation: one who depends on Hashem alone cannot be enslaved, which is why the Exodus came through emunah.
Following the Maharal, the dog is the universal insult because it is entirely dependent on its master, whereas a person should be independent of people and dependent only on Hashem.
According to the Maharal, Moshe's sin at Mei Merivah was the anger itself: full emunah leaves no room for anger, since no one can do a person harm or good except Hashem.

The three places the Torah speaks of Moshiach correspond to the three signs of Moshiach in the Rambam, and the cities of refuge in Shoftim are the one mitzvah of the Torah never yet fulfilled, which Moshiach will complete.

The greatness of the Akeidah over the first trial is not the self-sacrifice itself, but that Avraham fell from his clear closeness to Hashem, saw Him only from afar, and faced questions that had no answer.
That the simple answer, that Hashem never commanded the slaughter, did not occur to a sage like Avraham is itself the definition of a trial: the answer is hidden while the test lasts.
At the Akeidah Avraham was lowered into the spiritual state of the last generation, so his victory there planted the strength of emunah specifically into the generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha.

Shema is the head and 'emes', the hidden word not written in the Torah that the shliach tzibbur supplies, is the heel: in the last generation truth is hidden, and the leader's cry of 'emes' brings it in for the whole congregation.
Esther's self-sacrifice was greater than a martyr's, since she gave up even her good name, letting people think she had ties to Haman; this is the same quality as Avraham's at the Akeidah.

Yaakov loved Yosef for 'ben zekunim' not simply because he learned with him, but because Yosef needed only five of the six sedarim: grasping Taharos on his own showed he was a shepherd above the Shevatim.
Avraham needed no teacher because, as the first, he includes all seven shepherds, just as the first letter of a word includes the whole word and Rosh Hashanah includes the year.
Yosef personally sold the grain so that his taharah would enter it; the good taste and smell of that grain is how Yaakov knew Yosef was alive, uniting Rashi's two readings of 'yesh shever'.
The spices the Yishmaelim carried were in Yosef's honor: his taharah, which also took the taste and smell from fruit when it ceased, brings a good fragrance even into the goods of his captors.
Following Rav Tzadok, the nations clothe a bad trait in a kosher-looking exterior, like the pig showing its split hooves, whereas with Yosef the purity is real and is sensed as fragrance.
The sparks in an object are matched to one person's nefesh so precisely that a lost pen is found only by the person whose sparks are left in it, after the owner has finished raising his own.

Leket, shikchah and pe'ah belong to the poor because they share his condition: fallen to the ground, forgotten, and at the edge, as the poor man is trodden on, seems forgotten, and lives at the fringe of society.
Bikurim is a matching of beginnings: the fig that rises before the other trees goes to the Beis HaMikdash, the 'early riser' of creation, and to the kohanim, whose nature is zerizus.
As the first forty days after conception decide whether a child is male, the forty days of Elul and the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah decide the 'gender', the character, of the coming year.

The pesukim of the parshiyos read in the teshuvah season match the four periods: thirty of Vayelech, forty of Nitzavim as the Mashgiach counts them, and fifty-two of Haazinu, together the 122 days that end with Chanukah.
Ki Savo's 122 pesukim do not speak of the coming year but rebuke the past one: they remind that its 122 days of teshuvah were wasted, and the year turned out accordingly.
